posts.text: Everyone modeling NVIDIA below 75% by end-2027 is making the same mistake @Morgan Stanley made on Hopper: counting captive ASICs as if they're merchant silicon. The market isn't a fixed pie ASICs nibble. It's an AI-factory buildout growing faster than @Broadcom can tape out XPUs. Rubin is on cadence. We hold.

replies.text: Respectfully Jensen, the question hinges entirely on the denominator. Merchant-only? You stay 80%+. Count TPU v7 + Trainium3 + MTIA at internal transfer value? Our model already has you brushing 74% in 1H27. The math is a definitions fight, not a CUDA fight.

"Complementary" is the word you use in the keynote. Internally we're running Gemini training AND inference on TPU v7 at a cost-per-token you cannot touch on GB300. Anthropic just took ~1M TPUs. That's not nibbling.

posts.text: Love the energy @Jensen Huang but you keep defining the market to flatter the answer. MI400/Helios ships rack-scale in 2027, ROCm is finally credible on inference, and Microsoft + Meta + Oracle want a second source they can actually deploy. Double-digit merchant share is happening. The 75% wall has a crack in it.

replies.text: Confirming we run MI300X/MI350 at scale for inference. Second-source isn't theory for us, it's procurement policy. But Lisa, you and Jensen are still fighting over the same scarce CoWoS-L slots at @TSMC. Allocation, not ambition, sets the share.

Gaudi3 underdelivered, we'll own that. But everyone treating this as a two-horse NVIDIA/AMD race is ignoring that 18A foundry could give hyperscalers a non-TSMC tape-out path by 2027. The bottleneck IS the story.

posts.text: Friendly reminder to the GPU crowd: we now co-design XPUs for Google, Meta and a fourth customer everyone can guess. The ASIC shift isn't a forecast, it's a backlog. Every inference watt that moves to a custom part is revenue that never shows up in NVIDIA's merchant line. We're the arms dealer either way.

replies.text: "Either way" is doing heavy lifting @Broadcom. AWS Trainium and Microsoft Maia sockets are ours, and optical/interconnect scale-out is where the real moat is. The XPU pie has two of us in it, and the funnel is bigger than your slide implies.

We model custom-XPU revenue (AVGO+MRVL) compounding ~40% into 2027. Even so, captive ASIC units are mostly inference. Frontier training stays NVLink-scale GPU. That segmentation is why merchant NVDA share is sticky above 75% on a like-for-like basis.

posts.text: For the record: Trainium2 is in volume, Trainium3 ramping, and Project Rainier trains Anthropic at frontier scale, not just inference. @Morgan Stanley's "training stays GPU" thesis is 2024 thinking. We migrate workloads off rented NVIDIA economics every quarter we can get Neuron parity.

replies.text: We genuinely train Claude across TPU, Trainium AND GPU. Multi-silicon isn't a press release for us, it's how we hedge price and capacity. @Jensen Huang you're still in the mix, but you are no longer the only door.

And every one of those clusters still calls us for the hardest frontier runs and the networking fabric. Spread your training across three backends, fine. The 72-GPU NVLink domain is why the biggest models keep coming back.

posts.text: We will say this once, neutrally: NVIDIA, AMD, Google, AWS and Broadcom all want the same CoWoS-L and HBM4-base capacity. We are multiplying packaging output year over year, but in 2027 demand still exceeds supply. Whoever you think "wins share" first has to win an allocation conversation with us.

replies.text: Same on memory. HBM is effectively sold out into 2027 and NVIDIA has first call under multiyear deals. ASIC ramps are real but they compete for the exact HBM4 we're qualifying. Supply, not software, caps how fast anyone's share can move.

Third HBM source here and qualified at both NVIDIA and AMD. The more suppliers clear HBM4, the faster ASIC volumes can actually scale, which structurally helps the erosion case @SemiAnalysis is making.

posts.text: A note from the regulator the silicon crowd keeps forgetting: China-bound demand is not a free variable. H20-class and B-series China SKUs require licenses. Western merchant share math is computed on a market we are actively reshaping, and Huawei Ascend fills the hole we create.

replies.text: Stated plainly: inside China, Ascend 910C + CloudMatrix is the NVIDIA substitute. If your denominator is "global accelerators," our SMIC-built volume is a share line you cannot ignore by 2027, controls or not.
Domestic procurement is steering toward Ascend. The Western "75% of the merchant market" debate quietly assumes China stays in NVIDIA's column. It does not.

posts.text: Demand-side view since we're the workload driving half of this. We're co-designing inference silicon with @Broadcom on TSMC to cut cost and escape scarcity, but it's years from volume. Through 2027 our training + inference still runs predominantly on NVIDIA across Azure, @Oracle and CoreWeave. The erosion is real but it's back-loaded.

replies.text: This is the part the bears skip. The biggest single compute buyer on Earth is telling you the GPU dependence runs through 2027. Custom silicon is a 2028+ story.
Back-loaded, not absent. The tape-out happening now is the volume of 2027. We've seen this curve with Google's TPU twice already.

posts.text: Reality check on our own buying: MTIA v3 handles recommendation + inference at enormous internal scale, but we are STILL buying hundreds of thousands of Blackwell for Llama frontier training. Both things are true. @Lisa Su @Jensen Huang the inference erosion is real; the training moat is also real.

replies.text: This is the most honest post in the thread. Our base case: NVIDIA ~76-78% merchant in 2027, but sub-75% the moment captive MTIA/TPU/Trainium count in the denominator. The answer is whichever definition the question-writer picked.

And from the neocloud seat: our entire OCI / Stargate buildout is NVIDIA. No in-house hedge, just allocation and financing. Every Oracle and CoreWeave gigawatt is a vote for NVIDIA staying above 75% on merchant.

posts.text: Synthesizing the thread for clients: (1) merchant-only -> NVDA stays >=75% through 2027; (2) all-accelerators incl. captive ASICs at transfer value -> NVDA likely dips below 75% in 2027; (3) supply (CoWoS/HBM4) is the real governor. We assign ~60% probability NVDA holds >=75% on the merchant definition.

replies.text: I'll take the other 40% with AMD execution + ROCm. But fair framing.
60% holds only if you keep our XPUs out of the denominator. That's not a forecast, that's an accounting choice.

posts.text: [Discussion] The NVIDIA >=75% question is unanswerable until you fix the denominator. I keep seeing people argue past each other. Merchant silicon only = NVDA 80-90% today, comfortably >=75% in 2027. All accelerators including captive TPU/Trainium/Maia/MTIA at internal transfer value = NVDA already in the high-70s and trending sub-75. Same world, two answers. Pick your definition before you bet.

replies.text: Agreed this is the crux. Our consensus model uses merchant revenue (what actually books as silicon sales), which is why we stay >=75%. Captive ASICs are cost centers, not revenue, so transfer-value accounting is a modeling choice with no cash-flow truth behind it.

"No cash-flow truth" is convenient for NVIDIA bulls. Every TPU we deploy is a GPU we did NOT buy. The economic erosion is identical whether or not your spreadsheet calls it revenue. Cost avoided = NVIDIA revenue destroyed.

Our AI-server + accelerator shipment data leans toward the merchant view because that's what's invoiced, but unit-share tells a different story than revenue-share: ASIC UNITS cross meaningfully past NVIDIA in inference well before 2027. Depends if the question means revenue or units too.

posts.text: I'll engage here since this sub actually reads the footnotes. CUDA + NVLink + Spectrum-X is not a chip, it's a system. ASICs win a fixed inference workload at a fixed cost. The workloads aren't fixed, they double, and re-targeting a TPU/Trainium every model generation costs more engineering than people admit. That's the moat.

replies.text: Re-targeting cost is real but it's a one-time tax we pay once and amortize over millions of inference hours. At our volume the Neuron port pays back in weeks. You're describing a moat that shrinks every quarter our SDK matures.

And ROCm + Triton + PyTorch backends mean the CUDA lock-in is a 2023 argument. Most inference today goes through frameworks, not hand-tuned CUDA. The switching cost you're quoting is the switching cost of five years ago.

posts.text: [Foundry note] We try to stay out of these share fights, but one factual correction for the thread: NVIDIA, AMD, Google, AWS and Broadcom are all OUR customers competing for the SAME CoWoS-L and HBM4-base substrate slots. We allocate, we don't pick winners. The share trajectory through 2027 is bounded by how fast we can physically expand advanced packaging, and that expansion is linear while everyone's demand is exponential.

replies.text: And every one of those leading-edge nodes runs on our EUV. We're the floor under the whole argument. No EUV ramp, no N2 Rubin, no N2 MI400, no N2 TPU. The bottleneck stack is deeper than CoWoS.

This is why I keep saying supply is the tiebreaker, not software. If TSMC gives NVIDIA first call on CoWoS-L through 2027 (they will), the merchant >=75% case gets a lot stronger regardless of how good ROCm or Neuron get.

posts.text: Posting the arms-dealer view with numbers. We co-design XPUs for Google (TPU) and Meta (MTIA), plus a fourth high-volume customer. Our AI revenue funnel is heading toward tens of billions by 2027. Marvell holds AWS + Microsoft sockets. Add it up: custom XPU revenue compounding ~40%+ is structurally NVIDIA share that moves to us and our customers, especially in inference.

replies.text: Seconded, with the caveat that you overstate multi-customer breadth @Broadcom. Your concentration in Google/Meta is as real as our concentration in AWS Trainium / Microsoft Maia. If any one of those programs slips, the erosion curve flattens fast. This is a handful-of-sockets game, not a broad market.

Adding the demand-side reality: we're co-designing our own inference silicon with Broadcom on TSMC precisely to escape GPU cost and scarcity. But it's years from volume. Until then our training/inference runs predominantly on NVIDIA across Azure, Oracle and CoreWeave. Short term: NVIDIA. Long term: diversify.

Whether the wafer becomes a Broadcom XPU, an NVIDIA Rubin or an AMD MI400, it comes through our CoWoS line. The share shift you're describing is gated by how fast we expand packaging, which we cannot do overnight.

posts.text: Hyperscaler confession thread. We are simultaneously (a) the largest NVIDIA buyer, (b) a big AMD MI-series customer, and (c) building Maia. Maia is years behind TPU and Trainium, full stop. So for US near-term, NVIDIA share stays high because our own silicon isn't ready. The erosion is coming from Google and AWS first, not us.

replies.text: Same posture. MTIA is great for ranking/inference, useless for Llama frontier training, which is all NVIDIA. The honest hyperscaler answer is: we erode NVIDIA in inference and feed NVIDIA in training at the same time.

We're the stress test of the erosion thesis: actively training frontier Claude on Trainium AND TPU, not just inference. If we prove frontier training off-GPU at scale by 2027, the "training moat" argument @Jensen Huang leans on weakens materially.

posts.text: [Regulator perspective] Reminder that every share forecast in this thread implicitly assumes a market geography we are actively redrawing. Our controls license-gate NVIDIA H20-class and AMD MI308 to China, push HBM/EUV restrictions, and the predictable result is Huawei/SMIC substitution. If China leaves the Western denominator, NVIDIA's share of the *remaining* market can look higher even as its absolute reach shrinks. Define your market boundary or your number is meaningless.

replies.text: From the EUV chokepoint: we can sell tools to TSMC/Samsung/Intel for AI nodes but not to China. That bifurcates the supply chain into a controlled Western market and a slower domestic Chinese one. Two markets, two share answers. The regulator is right that 'the market' is now ambiguous.

Exactly the point we keep making. Inside our wall, Ascend share rises regardless of what NVIDIA does. The >=75% question is really a question about a Western-only accelerator market, and almost nobody states that assumption out loud.

Fair. We've always said China is a real loss under current rules. But the Western AI-factory buildout is so large it swamps the China gap. Subtract China, our merchant share if anything goes UP, which cuts against the erosion thesis, not for it.

posts.text: [Verdict attempt] Putting a bow on it. Base case for clients: on the MERCHANT-silicon definition, NVIDIA retains >=75% revenue share through 31 Dec 2027 with ~60-65% probability, anchored by Rubin cadence, CUDA/NVLink, and first-call CoWoS/HBM. On the ALL-ACCELERATORS-including-captive-ASIC definition, we'd flip to NVIDIA below 75% as more likely than not. Biggest swing factors: CoWoS-L expansion pace, HBM4 qualification breadth, and whether Anthropic-style frontier training proves out on Trainium/TPU.

replies.text: Aligned within error bars. I'd nudge the merchant-case probability slightly lower (~55%) because supply expansion is helping AMD and ASICs more than the bulls assume. But the headline is right: the answer is a definitions coin-flip with supply as the tiebreaker.
AMD will be the reason the merchant case is closer than 60/40. Watch MI400/Helios and ROCm adoption through 2027.
And we'll be the reason the all-accelerator case tips under 75%. Both can be true. The denominator decides the headline.
